newsitem.title: USA: Deep Blue digs deeper in third draw of chess match.
newsitem.headline: Deep Blue digs deeper in third draw of chess match.

text.p: The chess-playing supercomputer Deep Blue dug deeper into its database on Saturday to push world chess champion Garry Kasparov into accepting the third consecutive draw of their absorbing $1.1 million re-match.

Expert observers were stunned by the artful endgame strategy of the system, which marched its black king up the board to join a rook, knight and pawn in an attack as the Russian grandmaster threatened to convert a pawn into a queen at the other end of the board.

"It has widened the dimension of what's going on in these games," an excited international master Mike Valvo said. "It's increased the possibility of seeing computers change the game. They are going to show new ways of playing these complex endgames."

The draw after 49 moves and more than four hours of exciting, nerve-jangling chess for hundreds of spectators, chess experts and Kasparov, kept the six-game match tied after five games. Both players have 2-1/2 points after one win each and three draws. Game three on Tuesday and game four on Wednesday were also drawn.
Kasparov received several minutes of sustained applause and cheers from spectators as he appeared on stage in the auditorium of the Manhattan office complex where the games are taking place.

"There are very many discoveries in this match and one of them is that sometimes the computer plays very human moves," Kasparov said. "In a way I have to praise the machine for understanding very deeply positional factors. I think it is an outstanding scientific achievement."

Until now, chess-playing computers have favoured open, tactical battles where their massive calculating powers give them the advantage over human opponents. Deep Blue has shown in this match, which started a week ago, that it "understands" positional concepts.

"It was very, very close and I have to say it was a miracle that black escaped," said Kasparov, who sat at the board for some minutes after the game, gesturing and talking animatedely with his advisers and match arbiters.

"It's a tight match and tomorrow I will have to face another difficult challenge," said Kasparov, considered by most experts as the strongest player in the history of the ancient game. The final game of the match is on Sunday.
Playing with the white pieces and the advantage of the first move on Saturday, Kasparov chose the same opening king's knight move he used when he won the first game of the match last Saturday.

He sought to control the board's central squares in a formation known as the King's Indian Attack, shuffling a bishop five times in the opening 10 moves as the massive IBM calculating machine tried to turn the position in its favour.

Deep Blue is an IBM RS/6000 SP parallel processor with specialised microchips for chess that can examine hundreds of millions of possible moves per second. It made some unconventional opening moves with the black pieces without creating a major weakness for itself as it went into the middlegame, experts said.

But it was in the endgame that the machine surprised most of the experts as it coldly and precisely calculated the drawing variation. The computer's chess tutor, the U.S. grandmaster Joel Benjamin, said the programme "played very well and used its intuition, if you will, to see the position and it just went and made the most accurate moves."

The sixth and final game of the match was scheduled for Sunday. The winner will collect $700,000 and the loser $400,000 from the competition, a re-match following the human's victory over a weaker version of the machine in Philadelphia in February 1996.
Kasparov had two days since Wednesday's fourth game to recover psychologically and physically from three punishing games in which he resigned in a drawn position and then was held to two draws.
"I couldn't prepare normally, I played games three and four in a big crisis," Kasparov was quoted as saying in an interview on his Web site www.club-kasparov.com.

The event is part chess match and part research project to help build computers that can make complex, simultaneous calculations for applications such as weather forecasting, air traffic control and molecular dynamics, according to IBM.
